column4: The source section's root خ ش ع also names dry, sunken earth; here الأرض خاشعة until rain makes it stir and swell, then the ayah links revival to raising the dead.
The source section's dictionary gloss links خاشعة with هامدة; here earth is هامدة until water makes it stir, swell, and grow, evoking resurrection.
Wind drives clouds to a dead land; God brings out rain and revives the earth. This stages the section's rainless ground and its opposite.
Clouds are driven to a dead land, rain falls, and fruits emerge. The sequence directly fills out the section's dry-soil-to-life contrast.
The ayah says rain is sent to revive a dead land and water creatures; that is the life-giving water reversed by 88:5's boiling drink.
Water descends from the sky and revives earth after its death, the exact life-giving counterpart to the source section's dry land.
It directs attention to earth revived after death and calls God the reviver of the dead, spelling out the resurrection meaning of the soil scene.
Lightning, rain, and the revival of earth after death appear together, joining the source section's sky, water, and dry-ground images.
The source section's dictionary sense for good earth is soft and fertile; this ayah sends blessed water from the sky and grows gardens and grain.
The same rain scene continues with tall palms and clustered fruit, showing what watered, fertile land yields.
The rain-grown produce is provision, and the ayah says a dead land is revived; this completes the image begun at 50:9.
The source section's ن ع م dictionary branch names the moist southern wind; this ayah calls the wind sent to ʿĀd sterile (العقيم), a specific opposite.
The sterile wind leaves nothing it passes without turning it to decay, completing the opposite of the source section's moist, growth-giving wind.
The source section says the sky can name rain; this ayah sends measured water and revives a dead land with it.
The ayah says God sends water from the sky until the earth turns green, a visible reversal of the section's dried, dust-covered ground.
It names rain from the sky as what revives earth after death, directly joining the section's sky-and-ground images.
Rain brings green growth, grain, dates, grapes, and other fruit from the ground; this supplies the fertile-soil side of the section's image.
The ayah explicitly says God gives life to earth after its death, making the source section's dry land a sign of resurrection.
The source section's dictionary gloss allows samāʾ to mean rain; this oath names the sky as returning rain, paired with fissured earth in 86:12.
The oath names earth with fissures, a ground image paired with returning rain at 86:11 and apt for water opening dry soil.
Winds raise clouds and rain, after which people rejoice; the ayah stages the water-bearing sky that the source section hears in samāʾ.
Before rain, people are in despair; the next ayah shows the earth revived. This gives the section's dry/wet difference a human response.
Among signs in the heavens and earth, rain revives dead ground; this joins the source section's sky, land, and life-after-dryness images.
The sky supplies water for drinking and growth; this connects the source section's dictionary sense of samāʾ as rain to the land below.
The rain of 16:10 yields grain, olives, dates, grapes, and fruit, making the section's soft, good earth visibly fertile.
Water is sent down in measure and settled in the earth; the ayah adds that God could remove it, fitting the section's question of whether land receives water.
The settled water of 23:18 yields gardens of dates and grapes, showing the provision made possible by watered ground.
Rain makes the earth's growth lush before it becomes dry debris scattered by wind; the sequence links moisture, fertility, and drying.
Different plots are watered by one water yet vary in produce. The source section's soft-earth dictionary sense makes this a specific contrast in land's response.
A garden produces fruit and has a river running through it, a concrete watered-land counterpart to the source section's dry ground.
A garden may be struck from the sky and become slippery barren ground; this reverses the source section's soft, fertile earth.
Its water may sink into the earth beyond recovery, making explicit the dry-ground boundary in the source section's final sky-and-land image.
After the garden's water danger at 18:41, its fruit is destroyed and its trellises collapse; the ayah shows the cost of lost water.
Rain produces earth's growth, then it becomes dry stubble scattered by wind; this links the section's sky, soil, and changing surface.
Water is channeled as springs; crops grow, yellow, and crumble. This joins flowing water to the section's moist and dry ground states.
Rain-fed growth eventually yellows and becomes debris, extending the section's contrast between freshness and dryness to the life of plants.
Rain and the revival of earth after death are signs, giving the source section's dry soil a stated divine-significance context.
Rain comes after people despair and spreads mercy; the ayah links a dry, despairing state with water's relief.
Water is driven to barren land, bringing out crops for people and animals; this is a close picture of the section's dry ground receiving water.
If water sinks into the earth, who can bring a flowing spring? This names the boundary between the section's dry face and its running-water garden.
The ayah asks readers to look at earth and its many good growths, matching the source section's dictionary form for soft, fertile ground.
The ayah joins rain from the sky to gardens with rivers, fitting the source section's linked sky, water, and fertile-earth meanings.
Earth is made a bed and the sky a canopy, then water brings out fruit. This joins the source section's soft earth to its rain-bearing sky.
Earth is made a cradle, paths are laid, and water from the sky produces varied plants; this develops the source section's ground-and-rain pairing.
The ayah calls earth a cradle and gives paths through it; it shares the source section's attention to the formed ground.
Earth is made a resting spread, matching the source section's dictionary image of low, ground-hugging earth.
Mountains are set as pegs after earth is spread; this continues the formed-land scene that the source section pairs with sky and earth.
The seven heavens are built above the spread earth and pegged mountains, continuing the same sky-and-ground arrangement.
Clouds pour abundant water, giving the sky in the source section its dictionary sense of rain.
The rain of 78:14 brings grain and plants from the ground, showing what water does to earth.
The same rain sequence ends in thick gardens, completing the connection between the source section's sky and fertile ground.
The ayah asks who built the sky; the passage then turns to earth, water, pasture, and mountains, echoing the source section's gaze upward and down.
After the sky, earth is spread out; 79:31 names its water and pasture, completing a land-and-rain scene related to the source section.
Earth's water and pasture are brought forth, matching the source section's dictionary meanings of rain-bearing sky and good ground.
Mountains are set after earth's water and pasture; this continues the same created landscape considered by the source section.
The water, pasture, and mountains serve people and their livestock, completing the passage's account of the land's provision.
Rain is poured down abundantly, then the earth is split open; the following verses show the fertile growth of the source section's soft earth.
The ground opens after rain, making visible the soil's response that stands opposite the source section's dry land.
Grain comes from the opened earth, a concrete result of the rain-and-soil scene begun at 80:25.
Grapes grow from the watered earth, continuing the produce list that makes fertile ground visible.
Olives and palms continue the crops produced after rain, extending the source section's image of ground made fit by water.
Dense gardens complete the rain-grown landscape begun at 80:25, the opposite of dry, dusty earth.
Fruit and pasture continue the yield of the opened earth, showing its provision after rain.
The produce is provision for people and livestock, completing the rain-to-food sequence begun at 80:25.
Dust lies on faces in the same reckoning scene as the bright, laughing faces just before; this joins dusty earth and dusty faces as in the source section.
The source section links ناعمة to freshness and نعمة; this ayah says bliss's freshness is recognizable on faces, a direct positive counterpart.
The source section says سرير is named from سرور and describes sorrow-free joy; this ayah joins freshness نضرة with joy سرور.
Those who do good have no dust or humiliation on their faces, directly reversing the source section's dusted, bowed face.
Some faces are fresh on that day, directly answering the source section's pair of humbled and soft, fresh faces.
Other faces are grim on that day, the negative face-state paired against 88:8's freshness and the source section's softened face.
Some faces are bright in the same passage where others are dusty; this supplies a direct face-to-face contrast for the source image.
The bright faces laugh and rejoice, while the passage's other faces are dusty and gloomy; this clarifies the two outcomes in the source section.
Gloom covers faces next to the dust-covered faces of 80:40, continuing the source section's image of a crushed, dusty face.
The passage identifies the dusty, gloomy faces just described as disbelievers and sinners, adding the moral outcome to that scene.
The God-fearing are in Gardens and springs, a direct Garden-spring parallel to the source section's عين جارية.
The source section's dictionary gloss for سرير connects the couch to joy without grief; here rancor is removed and people sit on facing couches.
The source section names fatigue ناصبة; this ayah says no نَصَب touches the Garden's people, reversing exhausted labor.
The Garden's people say God removed their sorrow; this directly reverses the source section's dictionary sense of fatigue as grief leaving a mark.
The same Garden passage says no نَصَب or weariness touches them, directly reversing the source section's exhausted labor.
The source section's root ر ض و means the opposite of displeasure; this ayah repeats راضية مرضية for the soul welcomed into its Garden.
The source section has راضية for being content with one's effort; this ayah describes the good outcome as عيشة راضية.
The source section's root ر ض و means contentment; this ayah joins seeking God's pleasure to a garden that bears fruit under heavy rain or light dew.
The source section connects the word سرر to سرور; this ayah places the Garden's people on couches after saying they rejoice in God's gift and reward for their deeds.
The source section's dictionary explanation connects سرير to joy; this Garden scene places its people on couches, making that word-image concrete.
Raised beds in the Garden continue the source section's elevated couches and the ease opposite to laboring, exhausted faces.
The Garden's people enter with their spouses in joy, giving a concrete setting for the source section's soft face and couch named from delight.
The source section's ن ع م dictionary branch names a moist wind; the saved people say God protected them from the scorching punishment of samūm.
The source section defines عين as a spring; here the servants drink from a spring they cause to gush, opposite the boiling source at 88:5.
The source section's عين is a flowing spring; this ayah names a Garden spring, Salsabil, as a drink.
God gives the Garden's people a pure drink, the life-giving counterpart to the boiling water served in the source section.
The source section describes عين جارية; here two Garden springs flow, matching both the spring and its movement.
Two more Garden springs gush; this repeats the source section's spring image in a second pair of Gardens.
The Garden scene includes poured-out water, a flowing-water counterpart to the boiling drink and dry ground of the source section.
The God-fearing are in shade and springs, matching the source section's Garden spring as relief from hot, dry punishment.
The source section names عين as a spring; this ayah says the near ones drink from a spring, extending the fresh-face scene at 83:24.
The source section's root ن ع م names softness, freshness, and bliss; this ayah places the righteous in نعيم before describing their joy and couches.
They rejoice in what their Lord has given and been saved from; this is the satisfaction and joy that frames the couches at 52:20.
They are told to eat and drink gladly for what they did, joining reward for effort to the source section's satisfied face.
Abundant Garden fruit follows the poured-out water of 56:31, continuing the source section's image of provision from a watered, fertile setting.
The one given the record in the right hand returns to family rejoicing, a specific outcome parallel to being content with one's effort.
They eat and drink in satisfaction for what they did before, making explicit the effort-and-reward relation in the source section.
The source section's root ر ض و names contentment; this ayah says God is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him in Gardens.
The same root ر ض و from the source section appears in mutual pleasure with God, paired here with Gardens and lasting reward.
This ayah says God is pleased with the truthful and they with Him, echoing the source section's راضية face as contentment.
The source section defines ر ض و through the opposite of displeasure; this ayah uses mutual pleasure with God as the believers' outcome.
The contented soul of 89:28 is told to enter among God's servants, continuing the source section's movement from satisfaction to Garden ease.
The contented soul is finally told to enter the Garden, completing the same contentment-to-rest movement as 88:8–10.
The source section's root ن ع م names softness and bliss; the righteous are in نعيم in the passage that shows couches, fresh faces, and a spring.
They recline on couches in the passage that describes fresh faces and a spring, bringing the source section's couch and face images together.
A sealed drink follows the fresh faces of 83:24 and precedes Tasnim's spring, echoing the source section's joined face-and-drink contrast.
The Garden drink is mixed with Tasnim, leading into the spring named in 83:28 and extending the source section's running-water image.
The passage invites people to compete for this reward; this gives a specific effort-and-recompense parallel to the source section's satisfied face.
The ayah warns of a drink from boiling water as punishment; it is the source section's life-giving water turned into harm.
Disbelievers receive a drink of حميم; this hot-water punishment repeats the source section's reversal of water's life-giving role.
A drink of pus follows Hell; this is water supplied as punishment, reversing the source section's expected refreshment.
The drink is swallowed with difficulty and barely goes down, making the burning-water reversal of the source section bodily explicit.
Water like molten metal burns faces; this directly reverses water's expected refreshment and brings the source section's face image into the punishment.
Boiling water is poured over the heads of those in the Fire, the source section's drink turned into bodily torment.
The boiling water melts what is within them and their skins, specifying the bodily effect begun at 22:19.
After eating from the tree of Zaqqum, they receive a mixture of boiling water, joining failed nourishment to the source section's harmful drink.
The punished are dragged through boiling water and then fire; it repeats the source section's reversal of water into heat.
The tree of Zaqqum is food for the sinner, beginning a punishment passage whose drink and boiling heat mirror the source section's failed nourishment.
The tree is food for the sinful, specifying the failed provision that precedes the hot liquid at 44:45–48.
The food boils in their bellies like molten metal; this is a sharp opposite to the source section's expected nourishment and refreshment.
The food boils like water; this continues the heat image leading to the drink poured over them at 44:48.
Boiling water is poured over the sinner's head, a direct reversal of rain or a spring refreshing dry ground.
Hell is the place where they denied; the next ayah says they move between it and boiling water, the source section's water turned to punishment.
They circle between Fire and boiling water, exactly the burning-water boundary against the Garden spring in the source section.
The source section's ن ع م dictionary branch names the moist southern wind; this ayah gives the punished scorching wind and boiling water, reversing that freshness.
Their shade is black smoke, neither cool nor good; it sharpens the contrast between the source section's dry ground and fresh Garden.
The shade is neither cool nor refreshing, reversing the soft, pleasant condition of the source section's Garden faces.
They drink boiling water after their food, matching the source section's harmful drink rather than life-giving water.
They drink like thirsty camels, continuing the hot-water punishment begun at 56:54 and the failed relief in 88:5.
For the denier, the welcome is boiling water; this repeats the source section's drink turned into torment.
Burning in Hell follows the boiling-water welcome at 56:93, completing that punishment sequence.
In Hell they taste neither coolness nor drink, a direct boundary against the source section's soft, moist Garden.
The only drink is boiling water and foul fluid, making explicit the source section's reversal of water.
The boiling drink is requital, giving the hot-water scene at 78:25 its stated relation to deeds.
The righteous are given a drink blended with camphor, a cool Garden counterpart to the boiling drink in the source section.
A Garden drink is blended with ginger, continuing the pleasant drink opposite the source section's hot water.
The source section's root ن ص ب means fatigue; Moses says the journey has brought them نَصَبًا, an ordinary travel weariness parallel to ناصبة.
The source section's ن ع م dictionary branch names the moist southern wind; this ayah sends winds as good tidings before pure water descends from the sky.
The source section names ن ص ب for exhaustion and grief's mark; Job describes being touched by نُصْبٍ and suffering.
The source section's root خ ش ع describes abasement; here wrongdoers face the Fire خاشعين من الذل, with lowered, fearful eyes on Judgment Day.
The source section's root خ ش ع means bowing and abasement; here eyes are خاشعة on the Day, matching the humbled-face state.
Eyes are خاشعة on the Day of Judgment, repeating the source section's root خ ش ع in an eschatological facial expression.
The source section's root خ ش ع describes a lowered face; here eyes are humbled and disgrace covers them on the promised Day.
The source section's root خ ش ع evokes lowering; here people fall on their faces weeping and humility increases, a different but concrete posture.
The source section's root خ ش ع means humility; this ayah applies it to believers' prayer, a devotional rather than Judgment-Day state.
The source section's root خ ش ع means bowing; this ayah asks believers' hearts to humble at God's remembrance, extending the same inward posture.
The source section's root خ ش ع names a low, bowed condition; here a mountain would become humbled and split from fear of God.
Hardship and adversity strike earlier peoples so they might humble themselves; 6:43 supplies the same root as the source section's link from ضريع to abasement.
They do not humble themselves when punishment comes and their hearts harden; the source section links ضريع's root ض ر ع with abasement.
The source section explicitly links ضريع's root ض ر ع to humility; this ayah uses تضرعًا for humble supplication, a distinct setting of that root.
The source section connects ضريع's root ض ر ع to abasement; here hardship is sent so a town's people may humble themselves.
Hardship is replaced with prosperity in the next ayah, a specific reversal of the source section's dry and softened states.
Though seized by punishment, the people do not humble themselves; the ayah uses the root ض ر ع that the source section links to ضريع and abasement.
The fresh faces of 75:22 look toward their Lord; this adds their stance to the positive face-state parallel.
The grim faces of 75:24 expect a crushing disaster, explaining the negative face-state that contrasts with the source section's freshness.
Faces are blackened on the Day of Resurrection, another public face-boundary against the source section's fresh and softened faces.
The one given the record in the right hand receives an easy reckoning, the effort-and-outcome setting continued by rejoicing in 84:9.
The deafening cry marks the Day when the dusty faces of 80:40 appear; the cited verse supplies that scene's onset, not its dust.
The Garden reward follows patient labor, matching the source section's contrast between exhausted work and contentment with one's effort.
The Garden has no scorching sun or bitter cold; this gives the fresh faces and pure drink of 76:11–12 a climate opposite to torment.
The source section's dictionary form ناصبة names exhausting labor; this ayah denies لُغُوبٍ in creation, a possible but indirect boundary with human strain.
